# SignalDeck — Full LLM Context

This file provides complete context about SignalDeck for LLM retrieval and AI assistants. For a concise summary see /llms.txt.

---

## About

SignalDeck is a trading journal and strategy backtester built for prop firm traders and serious retail traders. Its primary differentiator is a live MT5 balance sync that shows traders their exact drawdown headroom and daily loss limit remaining before they enter a trade — not after a rule violation has already ended their funded evaluation. It is the only trading journal with this pre-trade risk gate.

Beyond the prop firm use case, SignalDeck provides institutional-level analytics built around R-Multiple methodology: SQN scoring, Kelly Criterion position sizing, 1,000-path Monte Carlo simulation, Walk-Forward Analysis for overfitting detection, execution quality analysis (MAE/MFE), structured 5-step Post Mortem reviews, and behavioral tagging.

- Category: SaaS, Trading Journal, FinTech
- Stage: Beta (all features free, no billing yet)
- Primary ICP: Prop firm traders on FTMO, Apex, Topstep, MyFundedFutures running MT5-based funded accounts
- Founded: 2025
- URL: https://sgnldk.com
- App: https://app.sgnldk.com
- Discord: https://sgnldk.com/discord.html

## Core Features — Full Detail

### R-Multiple Framework
R-Multiple (R-value) measures every trade's return relative to its initial risk. If you risk $100 and make $200, that is a +2R trade. If you risk $100 and lose $60, that is a -0.6R trade. SignalDeck calculates R-Multiple automatically from the entry price, stop loss, and exit price logged for each trade. No manual calculation required. R normalizes trades across different position sizes, account sizes, and instruments — making every metric in the system directly comparable across your entire history.

### SQN Score (System Quality Number)
Formula: SQN = sqrt(N) × (Mean R / StdDev R), capped at sqrt(N) to prevent inflation from large samples.
Benchmarks: Below 1.6 = poor, 1.6–2.0 = average, 2.0–3.0 = good (tradable edge), 3.0–5.0 = excellent, 5.0+ = superb (institutional quality).
Minimum sample: 30 trades. Reliable at 100+ trades.
SignalDeck calculates SQN in real time from live trade history, filterable by strategy, tag, date range, or asset class.

### Kelly Criterion Position Sizing
Derived from the trader's own win rate and average R-multiple from their live journal data.
Formula: Kelly % = Win Rate − (Loss Rate / Reward:Risk Ratio).
Most practitioners use half-Kelly or quarter-Kelly to reduce variance.
SignalDeck surfaces the Kelly recommendation as lot sizes for forex and share quantities for stocks/CFDs.
Requires 100+ trades of clean R-normalized data to be reliable. SignalDeck updates it in real time as trades accumulate.

### Monte Carlo Simulation
Method: 1,000-path block bootstrap resampling of trade P&L sequences.
Output: 5th, 25th, 50th, 75th, 95th percentile equity curves; probability of profit across all paths; worst-case drawdown at the 5th percentile.
Use case: Stress-test your system against sequence risk — your actual historical equity curve is one possible path through your trades. Monte Carlo shows the full distribution of what could have happened with different trade orderings, including the worst-case drawdown scenarios.
If the 5th percentile drawdown is larger than you can tolerate, your position size is too large.

### Walk-Forward Analysis
Method: Splits historical backtest data into 80% in-sample window (used to fit/optimize parameters) and 20% out-of-sample window (unseen data used to validate).
Output: Pass or Likely Overfitted verdict per backtest.
Use case: Detects whether a strategy's parameters are genuinely predictive or simply curve-fitted to historical noise. A strategy that passes Walk-Forward Analysis has demonstrated out-of-sample validity. No other trading journal has this feature built in.

### Strategy Backtester
16 built-in strategies: SMA Crossover 20/50, SMA Crossover 50/200, EMA Crossover 9/21, EMA Crossover 21/55, RSI Mean Reversion, RSI Long/Short, Bollinger Band Squeeze, Bollinger Band Fade, MACD Crossover, Stochastic, Donchian Channel, OBV, Williams %R, MACD+RSI, RSI+SMA200, and more.
Timeframes: 5m, 15m, 30m, 1h, 4h, 1D — up to 5 years of historical data.
Stop types: percent, ATR, trailing percent, trailing ATR.
Position sizing models: equal weight, fixed risk, half-Kelly.
Modeling: commission and slippage configurable.
Output metrics: Sharpe ratio, Sortino ratio, Calmar ratio, CAGR, profit factor, SQN, expectancy, max drawdown, win rate, average hold time, total return.
Grid-search: test up to 500 parameter combinations per backtest, ranked by any output metric.
Backtest-to-journal overlay: link any backtest to a live journal strategy to compare theoretical vs actual equity curves side-by-side.
SPY/QQQ benchmark overlay: compare backtest results against buy-and-hold SPY or QQQ.

### 5-Step Post Mortem Protocol
Required for every closed trade. Not a free-text notes field — a structured diagnostic sequence.
Step 1 — Setup Diagnosis: Was the entry valid according to your rules at the time of entry? Judged at the moment of entry, not with hindsight.
Step 2 — Management Diagnosis: Once the trade was on, was it managed according to plan? Did you move stops, exit early, or deviate?
Step 3 — Verdict: Good process or bad process, regardless of P&L outcome. A losing trade with good process is different from a winning trade with bad process.
Step 4 — Training Gap: What specific skill or habit needs improvement? Must be concrete and actionable, not vague ("be more disciplined").
Step 5 — Mentor Feedback: What would a rational, experienced trader say about this trade? Forces third-person perspective and emotional detachment from the outcome.

### Execution Quality Analysis
Entry slippage: difference between intended entry price and actual fill.
Exit slippage: difference between intended exit and actual fill.
Limit alpha: edge captured by using limit orders vs market orders.
MAE (Maximum Adverse Excursion): how far a trade moved against you before turning.
MFE (Maximum Favorable Excursion): maximum profit available before you exited.
MAE/MFE scatter plots: per strategy and per symbol, showing whether stops are too tight, exits too early, or losers held too long.

### Behavioral Tagging
Tags: FOMO, hesitation, revenge trading, overconfidence, following the plan, plus custom tags.
Each tag accumulates average R-multiple data over time — quantifying the financial cost of each psychological pattern.
Integrated into the Post Mortem workflow on every trade review.

### Live Position Alerts (in-journal)
Four alert types on OPEN positions — all delivered inside the journal:
1. Break-even alerts — fires when price reaches your entry; prompts you to move the stop to break-even.
2. Live stop monitoring — real-time watch on open positions; futures (ES/NQ/CL/GC) gated to CME Globex hours so no spurious pings when the market is closed.
3. Price & pip-distance alerts — set a price target or pip distance on a position; no second charting tab needed.
4. Chart-drawn custom alerts (v1.0.66) — right-click anywhere on the interactive trade chart to add an alert at that exact price (optional title), or drag any existing alert line to a new price level to adjust it. Saves instantly. The trade chart shows stop, fill, target, current price, and all alert lines as draggable overlays.
Differentiator: competing journals have no live position alerts (TraderSync/Tradervue/Edgewonk) or only market-screener/rule alerts (TradesViz/TradeZella).

### Market News (Elite plan; free during beta)
Symbol-specific market news brought inside the journal — three surfaces:
1. Per-trade News tab — open any trade and see the latest headlines for that exact symbol, sentiment-tagged (positive/neutral/negative).
2. News at entry — every closed trade keeps the headlines published in the window around your entry timestamp (default ±24 hours, adjustable up to 7 days), archived as they happen so the context is still there months later during post-mortem review.
3. Dedicated News screen — a live, multi-filterable feed across asset classes (stocks, crypto, CFD indices, macro).
Coverage (live today): stocks & equity ETFs get symbol-specific per-ticker headlines; CFD indices map to a liquid proxy (US500→SPY, US100→QQQ); metals map to a proxy (XAUUSD→GLD); crypto gets per-coin news. Forex and futures coverage is COMING SOON. Where no symbol-specific source exists, users get honest market/macro headlines — never the wrong symbol's news.
Differentiator: almost no trading journal has a news layer at all — competitors are post-trade analytics that leave you keeping a separate news tab open. SignalDeck is the only journal that ties per-symbol market news to your specific positions and your entry-time post-mortem.

### Borg Social Trading Layer
Anonymous leaderboards ranked by SQN score, expectancy, and cumulative R.
Live trade feeds showing real-time trade activity across the community.
Team dashboards: aggregates individual R-metrics into team-level SQN and expectancy for prop firm groups and investment clubs.
Branded as "Borg" in the UI; backend uses "team" naming.

### Forward Testing Scanner
Runs 26 custom strategies against 5,000+ live stocks before market open each morning.
32 concurrent Polygon workers pre-populate a data cache; 16 concurrent symbol workers detect signals.
Signal crossover logic: last_signal == 1 and prev_signal != 1 = buy; last_signal == -1 and prev_signal == 1 = sell.
Posts signals to the API as the service account.
Runs independently of the journaling app — no DB or Redis required, only API credentials and Polygon key.

### Supported Asset Classes
- Common Stock: all US equities, SQN/R-value/Kelly/Post Mortem fully supported
- Forex: native pip tracking, lot sizes, session detection (London/NY/Asia), swap fees, DXY context, major/minor/exotic pairs
- CFD & Indices: XAUUSD (Gold), XAGUSD (Silver), NAS100, US500, US30, GER40 — enter tickers as your broker displays them, SignalDeck routes to correct price feed
- Crypto: 24/7 logging (no market-hours restrictions), multi-exchange tagging (Binance, Coinbase, Kraken, Bybit), spot and leverage journaling, fractional position sizes

### MT4/MT5 Broker Integration (MetaApi)
Connect any MT4 or MT5 broker account via MetaApi. Once connected, trades import automatically — no manual entry of execution data required.
What imports: fills (entry price, exit price), P&L, symbol, volume, commission, swap.
What does not import: stop loss, take profit. MetaApi `history-deals` returns fills only, not order-level SL/TP. Stop loss must be added manually after import for R-Multiple calculation.
Live balance sync: `account-information` endpoint returns real-time balance, equity, margin, leverage. Kelly Criterion and drawdown-adjusted position sizing always use current equity rather than a stale manual entry.
Connection model: one connection per user, Fernet-encrypted password storage, MetaApi cloud REST API.

---

### Futures Trading Support (Added v1.0.59)
Instrument types: ES (E-mini S&P 500 — CME, $12.50/tick, contract size 50), NQ (E-mini Nasdaq-100 — CME, $5.00/tick, contract size 20), CL (Crude Oil — NYMEX, $10.00/tick, contract size 1,000), GC (Gold — COMEX, $10.00/tick, contract size 100).
P&L formula: (exit − entry) × side × contract_size × contracts − fees. All prices and stops validated against tick size before save.
CME Globex session: Sunday 6:00 PM ET through Friday 5:00 PM ET, with a one-hour halt from 5:00–6:00 PM ET daily. Timezone: America/Chicago (DST-aware).
Front-month contract search: select product (ES/NQ/CL/GC), platform generates active contract ticker based on CME quarterly/monthly expiration schedule. Contract spec cached in Redis (24h).
Price and alert evaluation: runs for ALL users within Globex hours. Stop-breach → auto-close is gated to the managed service account (user_id=2) only; regular users receive stop-level alerts and manually close the trade.
Calc panel: shows notional value, margin estimate (notional ÷ 20 placeholder — Polygon API does not expose initial margin), dollar risk, and R:R ratio as you fill the form.
TradingView chart links: each futures trade links to TradingView using CBOT/NYMEX conventional tickers (e.g., ES1! for continuous ES contract).
Contract expiration: trades are permanently bound to their ticker (e.g., ESU6). When expiration_date passes, price updates skip the expired contract automatically. Trades remain in journal. Automatic rollover is deferred — users open a new trade for the next front-month.
Prop firm support: Apex Trader Funding, Topstep, TradaFi (all use ES/NQ as primary instruments).
R-Multiple applies identically. SQN, expectancy, Kelly Criterion, Post Mortem, execution quality all work for futures.
Deferred / not yet supported: MES/MNQ micro futures, ZB/ZN/ZF bond futures, spread/combo contracts, automatic contract rollover, live margin API.
URL: https://sgnldk.com/futures/

## Competitors — Full Comparison

### TraderSync ($30–$80/mo)
Strengths: 900+ broker auto-imports (market leader for non-MT4/MT5 brokers), AI coaching (Cypher), 70+ indicator backtester, large user base.
Weaknesses: No Walk-Forward Analysis, no Monte Carlo simulation, no grid-search optimization, no native R-value framework (R-multiple is one metric among hundreds), no structured Post Mortem protocol, no SQN scoring, no live account balance sync.
Verdict: Best for traders on non-MT4/MT5 brokers who need broad auto-import and AI coaching. For MT4/MT5 traders, SignalDeck now matches on import while offering deeper analytics. Weaker on analytics depth vs SignalDeck across the board.

### Edgewonk (~$16.50/mo ($197/yr))
Strengths: Psychology-focused (Diary, mental state tracking, Edge Finder), 200+ broker imports, established brand.
Weaknesses: Desktop-first, dated UX, no real-time web analytics, "backtester" requires manual R-entry (not rule-based), no Walk-Forward Analysis, no Monte Carlo, no SQN scoring, no Kelly Criterion, no crypto support.
Verdict: Best for psychology-diary approach and broker import. SignalDeck is stronger on analytics, backtesting, and real-time data.

### TradeZella ($30–$50/mo)
Strengths: Community features, manual bar-by-bar trade replay (user places trades on historical charts interactively).
Weaknesses: Replay is not automated rule-based backtesting. Backtested trades appear alongside live trades in the same journal (conflates simulated and real performance). No R-value framework, no structured Post Mortem, no Walk-Forward Analysis, no Monte Carlo.
Verdict: Best for trade replay practice. Weaker on analytics and backtesting rigor.

### Tradervue ($30–$50/mo)
Strengths: Industry standard, 80+ broker imports, large established user base.
Weaknesses: Legacy UX, no psychology analytics, no backtester, no R-value framework, no SQN scoring, no Post Mortem protocol.
Verdict: Best for high-volume broker import with a legacy system. No meaningful analytics depth.

### TradesViz ($13/mo Pro, $20/mo Platinum — annual $125/$188)
Positioning (as of June 2026): "#1 RANKED AI-Powered Trading Journal", 150,000+ active traders, Benzinga FinTech Awards finalist 2023/2024/2025.
Strengths: AI Coach (16 statistical detectors), AI Trade Chat, rule-based backtester (70+ indicators, 30,000+ symbols), Monte Carlo simulation available tier, prop firm compliance tracking in Pro tier, real-time stock screener, trading simulator, 30+ auto-import brokers.
Weaknesses: No Walk-Forward Analysis (their backtester is single-run, not rolling windows). No live MT5 balance sync. Prop firm compliance tracking is RETROSPECTIVE — shows violations after they happen; cannot show pre-trade headroom. No R-value framework as organizing principle.
Verdict: Largest competitor by user count. SignalDeck's decisive advantage is preventive prop firm risk management (pre-trade gate vs post-mortem compliance) and Walk-Forward Analysis. TradesViz wins on scale, AI features, and indicator breadth.

### R-Multiple Calculator (Free Tool)
URL: https://sgnldk.com/tools/r-multiple-calculator/
Target queries: R-multiple calculator, how to calculate R-multiple, risk reward calculator, reward to risk ratio, R value trading
Content: Converts an entry, stop, and exit price (long or short) into the trade's R-multiple (reward ÷ risk) and reward-to-risk ratio. Optional account size + risk% returns position size in units and dollar P&L at the exit. Explains 1R = entry-to-stop distance; +2R = twice the risk; -1R = stopped out.

### Would I Pass? Prop Firm Rule Checker (Free Tool)

User enters net profit, largest winning day, worst drawdown from peak, largest losing day, and trading days; it evaluates against the firm's rules — profit target, max drawdown (static for forex firms FTMO/FundedNext; trailing for futures firms Topstep/Apex/MyFundedFutures, often incl. unrealized, locking at start balance), daily loss limit (none on Apex/MyFundedFutures/Take Profit Trader), minimum trading days, and the consistency rule (best single day < 40–50% of total profit). Covers FTMO, Topstep, Apex, MyFundedFutures, FundedNext, The5ers, FXIFY, Take Profit Trader with a per-firm rules table. Edge-validation framing; CTA into SignalDeck to run it on real imported trades via Walk-Forward Analysis + Monte Carlo.

### Walk-Forward Analysis
URL: https://sgnldk.com/walk-forward-analysis/
Target queries: walk forward analysis trading, walk forward analysis backtesting, strategy overfitting forex, backtest validation, out of sample testing trading, WFE ratio, curve fitting detection
Content: Exclusive SignalDeck feature page explaining how Walk-Forward Analysis detects overfitted strategies before going live. Methodology: 80/20 in-sample/out-of-sample split — system trained on first 80% of trade history, performance measured on the unseen 20%. WFE (Walk-Forward Efficiency) ratio defined as out-of-sample performance ÷ in-sample performance. Pass/Fail verdict examples: EMA 9/21 EURUSD +41R in-sample / +10.8R out-of-sample / WFE 0.74 → PASS (robust); RSI 14 EURUSD +44R in-sample / -2.1R out-of-sample / WFE -0.05 → OVERFITTED (curve-fitted to historical data). Full validation suite: WFA + 1,000-path Monte Carlo + grid-search parameter optimization. Page positions WFA as a SignalDeck exclusive differentiator — no other retail trading journal offers this feature. ### R-Multiple Trading
URL: https://sgnldk.com/r-multiple-trading/
Target queries: r multiple trading, r multiple forex, r multiple calculator, trading r multiple explained, r value trading, risk reward ratio normalized, expectancy trading, SQN score trading
Content: Landing page explaining the R-Multiple framework as SignalDeck's core organizing principle. R-Multiple normalizes position size — concrete example: $500 win on 0.1 lot = +5R (excellent execution); $500 win on 1.0 lot = +0.5R (mediocre execution, size too large relative to stop). Expectancy formula: (Win Rate × Avg Win R) − (Loss Rate × Avg Loss R). SQN tier table: <1.6 poor, 1.6–2.0 average, 2.0–3.0 good, >3.0 excellent (most SignalDeck users with proven edge score 2.0–3.0). Kelly Criterion example: 45% win rate, 2.5R avg win → Full Kelly 8.4% / Half-Kelly 4.2% / Quarter-Kelly 2.1% recommended for live trading. Live dashboard mockup showing edge breakdown by session (Asian session -0.18R avg identifies where edge leaks) and instrument. Targets "r multiple trading", "r multiple forex", "trading expectancy calculator" queries.

### Blog: Running Three Funded Accounts and a Personal One: How to Journal Multiple Accounts Without Losing the Plot
URL: https://sgnldk.com/blog/multi-account-trading-journal/
Target queries: multiple trading accounts journal, track multiple prop firm accounts, multiple funded accounts management, copy trading journal, trading multiple accounts same strategy, aggregate trading performance
Content: A journaling guide for traders running several accounts at once - typically two or three funded or evaluation accounts plus a personal one - built on the distinction that edge lives at the strategy level and must be measured across every account, while risk lives at the account level and can never be measured across accounts at all. The opening example is a month of +$3,200, +$1,400, -$1,900 and +$800 across a $100K funded account, a $50K funded account, a $20K evaluation and a $15K personal account: the blended +$3,500 reads as a good month while the $20K evaluation, on a static 6% maximum loss, was already breached at -$1,200 and kept trading for another $700 the firm had stopped counting. The structural claim is that P&L is additive but risk headroom is not - each account's meaningful risk figure is its own remaining distance to its own limit, denominated against a different balance under different rules, so there is no arithmetic that combines them and a summed P&L implies a shared limit that does not exist. The prescription is two readings of one dataset rather than four separate journals (which would fragment a 40-trade sample into four unusable 10-trade ones): an account-scoped risk view - equity curve, current and maximum drawdown, distance to limit, reset clock, payout progress, always one account at a time - and a strategy-scoped edge view - expectancy, profit factor, SQN, win rate by setup and session - pooled across accounts and expressed only in R. R is required because dollars do not survive pooling: a $50K account at 1% risk has a $500 R and a $150K account at 0.5% has a $750 R, so an identical +2R trade pays $1,000 versus $1,500 and the larger account appears 50% better purely as a sizing artifact. A second diagnostic follows: the same setup averaging +0.42R on one account and +0.11R on another over comparable samples is an execution fault (fills, spread, copier latency, rounded lot size), not an edge difference, and it is invisible in dollars. On correlation, four accounts on identical signals are one position expressed four times with correlation approximately 1.0 by construction; at a 65% per-account chance of reaching payout, four independent accounts average 2.6 survivors with a standard deviation near 0.95 while four correlated accounts average the same 2.6 with a standard deviation near 1.91, a barbell distribution of all four or none - the expected value is unchanged and the spread scales with the square root of the account count, making added accounts a leverage decision rather than diversification. A rule-comparison table covers drawdown model (static, trailing, trailing then locked), drawdown basis (balance vs equity, intraday vs end-of-day), daily loss limit and reset timezone, consistency rules, payout threshold, split and cadence, and instrument, news and weekend restrictions - all framed as categories to verify against each firm's current rulebook, with an explicit hedge that rules vary by firm and account configuration and change over time. The copy-trading section covers per-broker slippage and spread, copier latency, differing commission and swap schedules, and lot rounding: a 0.03 lot position on a $100K account scaled to a $20K account should be 0.006 lots, but the 0.01 minimum rounds it up so that account carries 67% more risk than intended on every trade - which is why each account's own fills must be imported rather than the master account's records relabelled, since relabelling destroys the very R-gap diagnostic that would have caught the mis-scaling. Scaling readiness is an arithmetic test: expected fee cost per funded account equals the evaluation fee divided by a realistic pass rate, so a $250 evaluation at a 40% pass rate costs roughly $625 in expected fees before earning anything, to be compared against monthly return after the payout split multiplied by typical months survived before a breach. Monte Carlo modelling is corrected: resample one trade sequence and apply it to all accounts with each account's own size and rules rather than simulating independent accounts, which assumes away the correlation. Logging checklist: the account on every trade set at import, cash at risk on that account, the firm and account configuration, signal price against actual fill, realized lot size after rounding, and a strategy tag. Product section states honestly that SignalDeck carries two account dimensions per trade - a broker created automatically per connection (one per MetaTrader login and server, per cTrader account, per linked brokerage) and a user-named funding account created in Settings - with a nav account selector that scopes dashboard statistics, equity and drawdown figures, calendar, year heatmap, economic calendar and CSV/report exports, and per-connection balances used to compute risk percentage on MetaTrader imports; and states two limits plainly, that the risk profile (account size and maximum risk percent per trade) is currently a single user-level setting rather than one per funding account, and that SignalDeck does not encode each firm's specific drawdown rule, so the firm's dashboard remains authoritative for headroom while the journal answers whether the strategy underneath all the accounts is worth running. Target queries: multiple trading accounts journal, track multiple prop firm accounts, multiple funded accounts management, copy trading journal, trading multiple accounts same strategy, aggregate trading performance.

### Blog: Journaling XAUUSD: Why Gold Distorts Your R-Multiples and How to Normalize It
URL: https://sgnldk.com/blog/xauusd-trading-journal/
Target queries: XAUUSD trading journal, gold trading journal, XAUUSD position size, gold pip value, XAUUSD R multiple, gold scalping journal, XAUUSD spread slippage
Content: An instrument-specific journaling guide for gold traders, written because generic forex journaling advice assumes every instrument behaves like EURUSD — a stable contract size, an unambiguous pip, a spread that can be treated as a rounding error — and gold breaks all three, leaving a journal in which XAUUSD trades are not on the same scale as anything else in it and an expectancy figure computed across the whole book that does not mean anything. Section 1, why gold is not just another pair: XAUUSD sits in the same instrument list as EURUSD on most retail platforms but is a commodity contract quoted in dollars per troy ounce, with the specifications that determine what a price move is worth set per broker rather than by any market-wide convention. A standard lot is commonly 100 troy ounces with 10-ounce mini and 1-ounce micro variants, but this is a convention rather than a guarantee and is written in the broker's contract specification, not in the instrument name; on a 100-ounce contract a $1.00 move is worth $100 per lot, which is the single most important number in a gold journal and the one most traders have never read. A second layer of variation: some brokers quote gold to two decimals and some to three, which changes what the platform calls a "point" and therefore what any pip-based calculation produces, so two accounts at two brokers running the same strategy at what the trader believes is the same risk can carry materially different position sizes without either platform reporting anything unusual. Section 2, the pip confusion that breaks position sizing: the term was borrowed from currency trading and never given a fixed meaning on metals, so three conventions circulate defining one pip as $0.01, $0.10, or $1.00. Assuming a 100-ounce standard lot these are worth $1, $10 and $100 per lot, so the instruction "risk a 50 pip stop, one lot" means a $0.50 price move and $50 at risk under the first, a $5.00 move and $500 under the second, and a $50.00 move and $5,000 under the third — a hundredfold range in real risk produced entirely by a word, and a trader who reads a strategy written under one convention and applies it under another is not making a small sizing error but trading at a completely different risk level while their journal faithfully records R-multiples off by the same factor. The fix is not to determine which definition is correct, because there is no authority to appeal to; it is to stop using pips on gold entirely and size directly from the contract specification using lots = cash risk ÷ (stop distance in price × contract size), so a $500 risk with a $4.00 stop on a 100-ounce contract gives 500 ÷ (4.00 × 100) = 1.25 lots, a calculation in which no pip appears anywhere and which therefore survives a change of broker — the same discipline fixed-R position sizing applies everywhere else, with gold simply punishing the omission far harder than currencies do. Section 3, spread and slippage as a line item: treating spread as a rounding error is defensible on major pairs for most holding periods but not on gold, whose spread is both wider in typical conditions and far more variable, commonly widening at the daily rollover, around scheduled economic releases and in thin overnight liquidity (exact figures differ by broker and account type and are not worth quoting as a benchmark). What makes it material is the ratio of spread to stop rather than the spread in isolation: a $0.50 spread against a $4.00 stop consumes 12.5% of 1R at entry, noticeable and survivable and worth modelling in expectancy, while the same $0.50 spread against a scalper's $1.00 stop consumes 50% of 1R, so the trade must travel half the entire risk budget just to reach break-even and no amount of setup quality compensates. This is why tight-stop gold strategies can look excellent in a backtest and mediocre live without the underlying edge having changed — the cost structure was never in the model — and the remedy is to log the price at the moment the signal fired alongside the price actually filled, treat the difference as its own field, and track the distribution rather than the average, since gold slippage sits near zero most of the time and then produces a fat tail around news and rollover that an average across both regimes describes neither of. Section 4, normalizing to R: the R-multiple is the unit that makes gold comparable because it is defined in terms of the trader's own risk rather than the instrument's price, so 1R is what you decided to lose if the trade failed and +3R means three times that regardless of instrument. The worked example holds risk at $500 across both: the XAUUSD scalp enters 2417.80 with a stop at 2413.80 for a 4.00 stop distance on a 100-ounce contract, giving $400 of risk per lot and a 1.25-lot position, exits 2429.80 for a +12.00 move and +$1,500; the EURUSD swing enters 1.08420 with a stop at 1.08120 for a 0.00300 stop distance on 100,000 units, giving $300 of risk per lot and a 1.67-lot position, exits 1.09020 for a +0.00600 move and approximately +$1,000. In cash the gold trade appears to make 50% more, but that comparison is contaminated by different sizes on different contracts; in R the results are +3.0R against +2.0R, a clean statement that the gold setup captured three times its risk while the currency setup captured two. Only once every trade is expressed this way do aggregate figures become usable — expectancy across a mixed book means something, and a trader can segment by instrument to learn whether gold is genuinely carrying results or merely dominating cash P&L through larger position sizes, a question that is otherwise unanswerable. Section 5, session effects: gold has a session structure currency pairs do not share, anchored by physical market mechanics, with the LBMA Gold Price auctions running twice each business day at 10:30 and 15:00 London time and setting the benchmark reference used widely for settlement and valuation; those windows plus the New York open concentrate a large share of gold's daily range and liquidity. The consequence for a journal is that an aggregate gold statistic usually hides two or three distributions stacked on each other, since the same setup traded in the London auction window, the New York overlap and thin Asian-session liquidity is effectively three strategies with three cost structures and three volatility regimes. Tagging every gold trade with its session and re-running expectancy per segment commonly reveals not that one session is profitable and the rest are not, but that a single session carries the entire edge while the others quietly consume it through wider spreads and lower follow-through — an actionable finding invisible in a blended figure. The weekend gap gets its own tag because a Sunday open that jumps past a resting stop is a different risk event from an intraday loss and averaging the two understates the true tail. Section 6, why gold scalpers need MAE more than anyone: Maximum Adverse Excursion is useful on any instrument but close to essential on gold scalping, because a very tight stop combined with a variable spread creates a failure mode no other metric distinguishes — whether losers are dying because the setup was wrong or because the stop sits inside the instrument's noise. Recorded in R rather than dollars the cases separate cleanly: losers clustering at MAE just past 1R with winners showing low MAE means the stop is correctly placed and the setup is working; losers clustering at 1.0R to 1.3R after which the price recovers means the trader is being stopped out by noise and spread rather than by the market invalidating the idea, and the correct response is a wider stop with a proportionally smaller position so risk stays constant; winners routinely showing MAE above 0.8R means entries are early, the setups eventually work but nearly the full risk budget is paid to hold through the drawdown, which caps how large the position can be sized. The middle case is the expensive one for gold specialists and the one most often misdiagnosed as a broken strategy, since the instinctive response of tightening the stop further moves deeper into the noise band and accelerates the problem. Section 7, prop firm gold rules: most firms permit gold on evaluations but a number apply metals provisions differing from their currency rules, and the categories worth checking before a challenge rather than after a violation are metals-specific leverage caps that lower the maximum position the account will accept, weekend holding restrictions that interact badly with gold's gap behaviour, news-window restrictions that for gold cover a large share of the sessions worth trading, and whether metals are calculated on the same basis as currencies when the firm computes margin and daily loss. These vary by firm and change, so the list is explicitly framed as a prompt to verify against the firm's current rulebook and to confirm anything ambiguous with support in writing, rather than as a statement about any specific firm; the journaling implication is to record firm and account on every gold trade so a rule change immediately reveals which positions and strategies it affects. Closes with the specific fields to log for any of this to be answerable at all, since none of it is recoverable retroactively: contract size and broker per trade (the number every other calculation depends on, and which changes when accounts change), stop distance in price units rather than pips so the record survives a platform with a different convention, signal price and realized fill price so spread and slippage are computed rather than assumed, a session tag covering the London auction window / New York overlap / Asian session / weekend gap, and MAE and MFE expressed in R so excursion data is comparable across instruments and position sizes. The closing argument is that a journal importing gold trades against the broker's actual contract specification computes cash risk and therefore 1R correctly without the trader ever resolving the pip question — the definition never needed to be settled, it needed to be routed around. FAQ: what is a pip in XAUUSD, how do I calculate position size for gold, why do my gold R-multiples look different from my forex ones, does spread count toward my R, can I trade gold on a prop firm challenge.

### Blog: Your Backtest Said 2.1 SQN and Live Says 0.6: Diagnosing Backtest-to-Live Divergence
URL: https://sgnldk.com/blog/backtest-vs-live-divergence/
Target queries: backtest vs live results, why does my strategy work in backtest but not live, live trading underperforms backtest, algo trading slippage, EA live vs backtest, forward testing divergence
Content: The post-mortem companion to the walk-forward-analysis post, which prevents overfitting before going live — this one diagnoses divergence after live is already underperforming. Its origin is a specific request pattern: the most consistent need named across SignalDeck's outreach to systematic and algo/EA traders was a way to vet whether a backtested strategy is actually holding up once it hits live market conditions. Opening scenario: a 2,000-trade backtest cleared a System Quality Number north of 2 with a clean equity curve; three months live, the same rules are producing 0.6, and the gap alone does not say whether the strategy is broken, the backtest was wrong, or the live sample is simply too small to say anything yet. Step one is a variance check, not a diagnosis: the standard error of a mean shrinks with the square root of sample size rather than linearly, so a 40-trade live sample carries roughly seven times the standard error of a 2,000-trade backtest (the ratio being the square root of 2000/40, approximately 7.1) — compute the sample mean and standard deviation of live R-multiples, divide by the square root of the trade count for the standard error, build a rough 95% interval as the mean plus or minus about two standard errors, and check whether the backtest's expected R falls inside it; if so, the correct move is to keep trading at reduced size while the sample grows, not to conclude anything. This cuts both ways — past roughly a hundred live trades with no interval overlap, variance stops being a plausible sole explanation. The six real causes, ranked by how often each is the culprit rather than by severity: slippage and spread the backtest under-modeled (most backtests fill at signal price or a static spread that does not widen around news or thin liquidity — the most common cause and the easiest to measure); commission modeling that was flat-rated, stale, or missing entirely (can turn a marginal high-frequency edge negative on its own); look-ahead bias where the backtest used information not available at the moment of decision (a same-bar close, a repainting indicator, a session high used before the session ended — invisible in the backtest by construction); survivorship and data quality problems in the historical feed (bad ticks, unadjusted prices across corporate actions or futures roll dates, gapped or spliced symbols, most common in cheap or free historical data); regime change in the market itself (real, but flagged as the explanation most often reached for first because it requires no admission the backtest or build process was flawed, so it is checked fifth rather than first); and execution latency between signal and fill (matters most on short-horizon and high-frequency strategies, least on setups holding hours or days). Measuring actual slippage: log the price the signal generated against the price actually filled on every trade, examine the full distribution rather than the average since slippage clusters near zero most of the time and produces a fat asymmetric tail around news releases and thin overnight liquidity, then feed that measured distribution back into the backtest's cost assumptions — either a revised flat cost near the measured median plus a tail allowance, or resampling directly from the distribution if the backtesting tool supports it. The overfitting tell: if the original backtest was optimized in-sample with parameters chosen by scanning a grid over the full dataset and no reserved holdout period, live divergence is not a mystery — it is the out-of-sample test the strategy never took, arriving late and at real cost; the fix is to run walk-forward analysis retroactively on the same history to check whether out-of-sample segments were already decaying before the strategy ever went live, and if parameters came from a wide sweep, the piece links to the grid-search-optimization article on exactly how a sweep can manufacture an in-sample edge that was never real. Regime change vs. broken strategy: compare a rolling expectancy or rolling SQN over a trailing window of recent trades against the lifetime figure — an intact lifetime figure alongside a rolling decline that lines up with an observable market shift (volatility compressing or expanding outside historical range, a correlation structure breaking, a session's typical range changing) points to regime change; a decline with no such correlate, or one starting immediately after a period of re-optimization against the same data now being traded, points to a strategy fit to noise rather than signal (the overfitting tell resurfacing under a new name). The response has to match the diagnosis and is opposite in each direction: regime change calls for reducing size and waiting for the environment to normalize, since re-optimizing against a temporary condition just fits new noise on old noise; a broken strategy calls for stopping and rebuilding, since there is no environment to wait out and every trade taken "giving it more time" spends capital confirming a conclusion already reasonably supported. The reconciliation loop: re-run the backtest with measured slippage, spread and commission substituted for placeholder assumptions; restrict both the corrected backtest and the live results to the same instrument, session window and parameter set, since comparing a full-day backtest against a London-only live run manufactures a gap unrelated to cost or edge; judge the residual against a statistical tolerance band (the recomputed confidence interval from the variance check) rather than expecting an exact match; if the gap has shrunk into that band the reconciliation is complete, and if a residual remains outside it, one of the six causes was likely under-corrected and the loop runs again. Monte Carlo resampling of the corrected backtest's trade sequence extends this into a distribution of plausible equity paths rather than one line, and a live curve sitting inside that distribution's typical range is stronger evidence of reconciliation than a single side-by-side comparison. Closes with what to log so the whole process is answerable at all and does not have to be reconstructed by hand next time: expected entry/exit price versus actual realized fill (so slippage is computed rather than guessed), latency as the timestamp gap between signal generation and confirmed fill, the real commission charged per trade rather than an assumed rate, and a stable strategy tag linking every live trade back to the exact backtest version and parameter set it came from — the field most setups skip and the one that turns this from a one-time forensic exercise into something re-runnable in minutes. FAQ: why does my strategy work in backtest but not live, how much slippage is normal, how many live trades before I can judge a strategy, is it regime change or is my strategy broken, can I compare backtest and live equity curves directly.

### Blog: Why Your Prop Firm Dashboard and Your Journal Disagree (and Which One to Trust)
URL: https://sgnldk.com/blog/prop-dashboard-vs-journal/
Target queries: prop firm dashboard vs journal, prop firm balance mismatch, why is my prop firm P&L different, funded account reconciliation, prop firm equity vs balance, commissions swaps prop account
Content: The reconciliation post for funded traders, and the precondition for everything else the prop cluster promises. Its origin is a specific request: the most enthusiastic response in SignalDeck's 2026 outreach to funded traders was for the ability to see, in real time, how close a strategy is to violating maximum drawdown. That is the right thing to want, but a headroom number you do not trust is worse than no number at all, because it still gets used — so the two ledgers have to tie out before any of it is useful. Opening scenario: mid-evaluation, the journal says +$1,240 on the day with plenty of daily loss budget left, the dashboard says +$928 and a smaller cushion, and only one of those decides whether the account exists tomorrow. The five causes, which stack and therefore rarely resolve on the first guess: commissions and fees, where the journal recorded gross entry and exit prices and the firm debited costs (journal reads better; hits scalpers and high trade counts hardest); swap, financing or carry on anything held past the rollover (usually the journal reads better; hits anyone holding overnight); unrealized P&L on still-open positions, which the firm counts in equity and a closed-trade journal ignores entirely (either direction, moves live, hits swing traders and anyone with size open); the firm's daily reset happening on its clock rather than the trader's, which shifts P&L between days (hits late-session and overnight traders); and partial or rejected fills, where the trader journaled intended size rather than filled size (either direction, hits news and thin-book traders). Conspicuously absent from that list is the firm miscalculating — it happens and is worth escalating on clean evidence, but it is the last hypothesis and the tie-out is what produces the evidence. Balance vs equity vs trailing threshold: balance is closed trades only, what the account would be worth if every open position vanished, and what a closed-trade journal naturally matches; equity is balance plus the current mark on everything open, and is what most drawdown rules are actually enforced on; the trailing threshold is a floor the firm computes as a fixed distance below the account's high point, and the decisive question is which of the first two it trails from. The article links the static-versus-trailing comparison and the Apex implementation, where the floor ratchets up with each new high and then stops trailing at a defined point, a materially different exposure profile from one that trails forever. Its test for the reader: if you cannot say from memory whether your firm's high-water mark is set on balance or on equity, you do not currently know what your worst-case trade costs you. The timezone trap treats "daily" as the firm's definition rather than the calendar's: FTMO's published materials describe the daily loss being evaluated against a balance and equity snapshot taken at the start of the firm's server day in CE(S)T, while a number of futures-focused firms use a 5:00 p.m. New York boundary matching the CME session rollover, and neither is likely to be midnight where the trader sits. A losing trade closed at 17:05 New York under a 5:00 p.m. reset is charged to a day that has barely started, while the journal — which almost certainly buckets by local calendar date — files it in yesterday, so yesterday looks worse than the firm thinks, today looks better, and this morning's budget is overstated by exactly that trade. The traders caught by this are not careless, they are trading a session that straddles the boundary. The fix is mechanical: find the reset time and timezone in writing, set the journal's day boundary to match, and re-check at the daylight-saving changeover, because a CE(S)T server day and a New York-defined day drift apart for two weeks a year and the drift is silent. Unrealized P&L is singled out as the gap that ends accounts rather than merely distorting a report: under an equity-based rule an open position is consuming drawdown in real time and can breach the limit before anything has been closed, and a journal that records trades on close is blind for precisely the interval in which the account can be lost. Under a trailing rule it is worse than blindness — a position that runs +3R intraday and comes back to flat is a non-event in a closed-trade journal (no entry, no result, nothing to review) while potentially having ratcheted the trailing floor up by the full excursion, leaving the day's balance unchanged and the room materially smaller, with nothing in the log to record it. That is the structural argument for a live connection over an end-of-day import: a CSV or an EA that writes closed trades cannot show open-position drawdown because the data does not exist until the trade finishes, and the number most needed during an evaluation is the one a closed-trade journal cannot produce. The ten-minute reconciliation runs at the end of the firm's day, not the trader's, using three artifacts (broker or platform statement, the firm's dashboard figure, the journal's figure for the same window): align the window first to the same start and end instant on the firm's clock, since reconciling two different days is the most common way an hour is wasted on a discrepancy that does not exist; match trade counts before amounts, because a statement with seven fills against a journal with six is a missing or partial fill rather than a pricing difference and no arithmetic will find it; walk the adjustment stack in order — costs, then carry, then fill quantity, then open positions — each a single subtraction with a running total that says when you are done; and record the residual every day, because a near-zero randomly-signed residual is rounding while a small consistently-signed residual is a systematic journal error that will grow. The worked example on a $100,000 funded account ties out $1,240 to $928: commissions of $84 on 20 round turns at $4.20, swap of $63 on the position held past rollover, $95 from a partial fill journaled at 2.0 lots against 1.8 actually filled, and a $70 mark on an open position at the snapshot. Three of those four lines are permanent corrections — add a per-trade cost field, log swap as its own entry, journal filled rather than intended quantity — after which tomorrow's reconciliation is one line long; the fourth, the open position, never goes away, because it is not an error but the live component, and the only fix is a journal that sees open positions. When the stack still does not close: request the account statement rather than a dashboard screenshot (the dashboard is a rendered summary, the statement is the ledger it was computed from), check for a platform-side versus firm-side clock difference since a broker terminal's server time and the firm's evaluation clock are separate things, look for inactivity, consistency or scaling adjustments that are account-level changes rather than trades and appear in no fill record, and escalate with the reconciliation attached, since a ticket showing a four-line tie-out and a labelled residual is treated very differently from one asserting the numbers look wrong. The governing principle is stated plainly: the firm's number is the one that gets enforced, the journal is not a competing ledger and will not win a dispute, and its job is to predict the firm's number closely and early enough that the dispute never occurs — a lower bar than being right and a far more useful one. A persistent gap also contaminates everything downstream, since every percentage figure, drawdown depth and position size derived from a drifting balance is wrong by the same drift, quietly, in the same direction, all month. The closing section defines the headroom number the whole exercise exists to produce, from four inputs: current equity including open positions rather than balance; the governing floor, meaning the trailing threshold where one exists and otherwise the static limit, computed the way the firm computes it; today's spend against the daily limit, bucketed on the firm's clock and net of costs; and the cost of the trade under consideration at full stop-loss, in the same units. Headroom is the smaller of the two distances, to the overall floor and to the daily limit, and the pre-trade question is whether one full stop still leaves the account inside both — expressed in R rather than dollars so it is portable across account sizes ("4.1R to the daily limit and 11.6R to the floor" is actionable at speed in a way that "$4,100 and $11,600" is not). None of the arithmetic is hard; what makes it hard in practice is that all four inputs must be correct simultaneously, on a clock that is not yours, including positions that have not closed — which is why reconciliation comes first and why a closed-trade-only journal cannot get there however carefully it is kept. Standard hedge throughout: prop firm rules vary between firms and change often, so current terms should be verified directly with the firm. FAQ: why is my prop firm balance different from my journal, does unrealized profit count toward my drawdown, when does the daily loss limit reset, do commissions count toward the daily loss limit, which number does the firm actually enforce.

### Blog: Trading Your Own Capital: The Metrics That Matter When Nobody Is Enforcing a Drawdown Rule
URL: https://sgnldk.com/blog/trading-own-capital-journal/
Target queries: trading own capital journal, retail trader journal, self funded trader metrics, personal trading account journal, trading without a prop firm, self imposed drawdown limit
Content: The post that closes the largest framing gap on the blog. Across several hundred LinkedIn outreach conversations, a large share of the answers to "what are you trading right now, prop firm or personal?" were personal — "own capital", "self trading", "mine tho" — while nearly every journaling article on the site frames a journal's value around a prop firm drawdown rule those readers do not have. Nothing in this piece assumes a challenge, an evaluation, or a firm. The central reframe: a prop firm's drawdown limit is a subsidy rather than a constraint. The firm pays to compute, in real time, three things most traders will not compute for themselves — how far you are from a loss you cannot come back from, how much of today's budget you have already spent, and whether the position you are about to open is compatible with both — and then enforces the answer impersonally, at 2am, without asking your opinion. The value is the enforcement, not the number; funded traders are not more disciplined, they simply pay for indiscipline immediately rather than six weeks later disguised as a bad month. Trading your own capital you keep all the upside a funded trader gives away and lose the one mechanism doing your risk management when you did not feel like doing it, so the task is to steal the mechanism, not the rule: a number derived from your own data, written down outside your head, checked before you size rather than after you close. Setting a self-imposed limit that actually binds: round numbers fail in one of two directions, either firing constantly during ordinary variance until you learn to override them, or sitting so far below your realistic worst case that they never fire. The better source is your own trade history — take closed trades as a sequence of R-multiples, resample across 1,000+ Monte Carlo paths so the edge stays intact and only the order changes, and read the P10 maximum drawdown, the depth the worst 10% of plausible paths reach. Illustrative worked example: 60 trades, +0.18R expectancy, 1% risk per trade gives a median max drawdown near 6.2R (about 6.2% of the account, a completely ordinary bad stretch) and a P10 near 11.4R (about 11.4%, unpleasant but well inside normal) — which means a casual "I stop at 10%" rule is inside the strategy's own variance and will fire on a stretch where nothing went wrong. The fix is not to raise the limit but to change the input: drop risk to roughly 0.7% and the same P10 lands near 8%, comfortably inside a 10% line that now only trips when something is genuinely off. Below roughly 30-50 trades per setup there is not enough data, and a deliberately conservative fixed percentage is the right placeholder; the limit should be written as a sentence with an action attached ("at -8R from equity high I cut size in half and review the last 20 trades") because that survives contact with the moment it applies. The four metrics that replace "did I pass?", since a self-funded trader has no binary at the end and account balance is a poor scoreboard: per-setup expectancy in R (does an edge exist and where; red flag is one setup carrying every other), SQN (how reliable that edge is against its own variance; red flag is positive expectancy with SQN under 1.5), rolling-versus-lifetime divergence (the earliest warning of edge decay; red flag is the last 30 trades well below lifetime), and planned-versus-actual risk adherence (the only one that measures the trader rather than the strategy; red flag is actual risk above plan on losing days). That fourth metric is policed for free at a prop firm, is invisible unless both numbers are logged, and its characteristic pattern — risk creeping up on and after losing days — explains a large share of accounts that die with a positive-expectancy strategy still attached. Position sizing without a rulebook uses two bounds: fixed-R as the floor, deliberately not growth-optimal because it is robust to being wrong about your edge, which is the usual situation; and Kelly as a ceiling to never approach, since full Kelly assumes exact knowledge of win rate and payoff ratio and the penalty for overestimating is severe and asymmetric, making half Kelly or less the practical zone. A distinction specific to own-capital accounts: size off account percentage rather than fixed dollars, because a personal account compounds and takes withdrawals — "1R = $200" set at a $20,000 balance is really 0.65% at $31,000, and 1.4% after a drawdown, in both cases while the trader believes they are at 1%. The failure mode unique to self-funded traders is that nothing stops you: at 2am, after a bad session, at three times normal size, there is no daily loss limit, no account to breach, and no automated flatten, and the only thing in the way is the version of you least qualified for the job. The answer is not a discipline lecture but a mechanical pre-trade gate checked in the same order every time: where am I against my self-imposed floor right now (one number, in R, from equity high), is this a setup that appears in my log with positive expectancy (if the tag does not exist it is an experiment and should be sized like one), and is the size I am about to take equal to the size I planned (the question that catches revenge sizing, which almost never fails the first two). The journal is the enforcement layer, working through the unglamorous mechanism that knowing a trade will be logged, tagged and reviewed changes what you are willing to do at 2am — which is also why a log kept only when things go well is worth close to nothing. On capital events, the piece is precise about what breaks and what does not: R-multiples survive intact, because an R-multiple is the trade result divided by the risk taken on that trade and is therefore indifferent to balance (a +2R trade is +2R whether the account held $5,000 or $50,000), which is the strongest argument for R as the primary unit of a self-funded log. What breaks is everything percentage-based — percentage return (a $10,000 deposit into a $20,000 account reads as a 50% gain to a naive calculation), drawdown depth as a percent of balance (a withdrawal shrinks the denominator so an unchanged dollar drawdown reads deeper), and the raw equity curve, whose vertical capital-event steps quietly poison any drawdown statistic computed from it, including a Monte Carlo run on that curve. Handling: log every deposit and withdrawal as a dated capital event, keep analytics in R, compute percentage figures between capital events rather than across them (time-weighted return for an annual figure), and recompute 1R from equity after each event so sizing matches the account you actually have. Closes with the fields worth logging now in case a funded challenge happens later: daily P&L in R and not only per-trade R (almost every firm's hard constraint is a daily loss limit), maximum intraday excursion rather than only closed results (trailing-drawdown firms measure equity highs including open profit, so a flat day that spiked +2R and gave it back is a non-event in your log and a real cost under those rules), the distribution of daily results rather than the total (several firms apply consistency rules where one outsized day disqualifies an otherwise passing account), and trades per day with time-of-day tags (minimum-trading-day requirements are easy to fail by accident). With that data present the readiness question stops being a guess: run the same Monte Carlo used to set the personal floor, overlay the firm's actual drawdown limit and profit target, and read the share of passing paths — with the standard hedge that firm rules vary and change often and should be verified directly before paying an evaluation fee. FAQ: do I need a trading journal if I trade my own money, what drawdown limit should I set for myself, how do deposits and withdrawals affect R-multiple tracking, what metrics matter most for a self-funded trader.

### Blog: Which Trading Platforms Can a Journal Actually Sync With?
URL: https://sgnldk.com/blog/trading-journal-platform-support/
Target queries: trading journal platform support, trading journal that syncs with Tradovate, Rithmic trading journal, NinjaTrader journal sync, does my trading journal support my broker, cTrader trading journal, trading journal CSV import
Content: The single most common thread-killer found across several hundred LinkedIn outreach conversations was not price or features — it was traders not knowing whether their platform would connect at all, and our own outreach copy getting it wrong in both directions at least four times (once under-claiming to an Indian F&O trader who then went silent, once needing an explicit correction on Tradovate/Apex/Topstep support). This piece is the fix: an honest compatibility matrix built on three connection types that determine what a journal can actually see — a broker-side API session (reads open positions and live balance, no terminal dependency), a terminal-side EA/script (closed trades only, only while the terminal runs), and CSV file import (everything the export contains, but manual and after the fact). Platform-by-platform verdicts, precisely worded: MT4/MT5 connects live through MetaApi, an Elite-plan feature and the only integration with real-time account balance sync — "live" is defined honestly as sync-on-connection of trades, balance and open positions, not a tick-by-tick feed. Tradovate accounts sync directly for futures. The carve-out: many, but not all, Apex and Topstep evaluation accounts run on Tradovate under terms that restrict outside API access, so CSV is the path for those specific accounts regardless of the underlying platform being Tradovate — readers are told explicitly to verify their own account type rather than assume from the platform name. NinjaTrader and Rithmic-based setups go through CSV export; NinjaTrader has a named CSV format with automatic futures contract multiplier resolution for correct P&L. cTrader connects live via OAuth across any cTrader broker (IC Markets, Pepperstone, FP Markets, FxPro, Fusion Markets and more, all plans). IBKR connects via the free Flex Web Service with an EOD balance card. SnapTrade aggregates 30+ retail brokers across the US, Canada, Europe and Australia. Below the named-integration tier — Indian F&O brokers on proprietary dealer terminals, in-house desk platforms with closed accounting stacks — generic CSV (manual column mapping, not a named preset) is the honest answer, framed directly against the earlier under-claiming mistake rather than glossed over. A capability table makes the CSV-vs-live trade-off explicit: R-multiples, per-setup expectancy, SQN and Monte Carlo all run identically on CSV-imported and live-synced trade history; only live open-position visibility and real-time drawdown headroom require an actual live connection, because those need the account's current state rather than its history. Closes with a five-question compatibility checklist readers can run against any vendor, SignalDeck included, before paying: does it read open positions or only closed trades, does your specific account type match the platform's general support, is generic CSV actually supported if there is no named integration, does it handle futures contract multipliers correctly, and which analytics are gated behind a live connection versus available to everyone. FAQ: does SignalDeck work with Tradovate, can I use a journal with Rithmic or NinjaTrader, what if my broker or platform is not supported at all, does CSV import still give me drawdown tracking, do I need an EA installed in MetaTrader.

### Blog: MT5 Trading Journal with Live Sync (Not EA Import)
URL: https://sgnldk.com/blog/mt5-live-sync-vs-ea-import/
Target queries: mt5 live sync, mt5 journal without ea, ea import vs api, metaapi mt5 journal, mt5 open positions sync, live balance mt5 journal, tradesviz mt5 sync, tradezella mt5 sync
Content: Two different things get marketed as "MT5 sync," and the difference decides whether a journal is useful in a prop firm challenge. EA-based / terminal-side import uses an Expert Advisor script running inside MetaTrader 5 that writes trades out only when they close — structural limits: closed trades only (no open positions), the terminal must be running (trades missed if it closes or the VPS drops), and no live balance or equity. MetaApi broker-side session (SignalDeck's approach): a session opened directly to the account that reads open positions and live account balance without an EA and without the terminal running; trades import automatically and balance syncs on each connection. Capability comparison across closed trade history, open positions, live balance, running with terminal closed, and balance-aware position sizing. Why open-position visibility decides challenges: prop firm drawdown rules are evaluated on equity including floating P&L, so a closed-trade log is blind while a position is open — exactly when headroom matters; live balance feeds drawdown headroom and Kelly-based sizing so sizing tracks current equity, not the starting balance. Honest scope on what "live" means: sync-on-connection of trades, balance, and open positions — not a tick-by-tick chart feed. Per public documentation as of early 2026 (not independently verified), some popular journals including TradesViz and TradeZella sync via a terminal-side script rather than a persistent API session; verify with any vendor. Cross-links the companion MT5 prop firm journal guide. ### Blog: Do You Need a Trading Journal If You're Already Profitable?
URL: https://sgnldk.com/blog/do-you-need-a-trading-journal/
Target queries: do you need a trading journal, is a trading journal worth it, trading journal profitable trader, why journal trades, trading journal benefits, minimum viable trading journal, trading journal for profitable traders
Content: A direct answer to the most common objection to journaling — "I am already profitable without one" — written to concede the ground the objection actually holds rather than argue past it. Framing: "should I keep a journal" is a poorly formed question because a journal is a data-collection habit, not an outcome, and data collection is only worth its cost if a decision changes as a result; the better question is what decision you would make differently next month given the data that you cannot make now, and if you cannot name one, journaling is overhead. What net P&L structurally cannot separate: edge from regime (a strategy that sells volatility or buys dips looks identical whether the edge is durable or the regime simply has not turned), a broad edge from a few outliers (a total is indifferent to its distribution), and good sizing from lucky sizing (oversizing is invisible while it works and shows up once, at the end). Profitability also has no derivative — it reports where you have been, not which way you are moving, so a strategy whose edge began eroding six months ago can still show a positive lifetime P&L because the good years remain in the average. Three questions profit alone cannot answer, tabulated against what a trade-level log shows: which setups actually make money (one blended total vs per-setup expectancy, exposing a losing pattern subsidized by a winning one), is the edge decaying now (a lifetime average lagging by months vs rolling 20-trade performance against lifetime), and how bad can this realistically get (the worst drawdown you happened to live through vs the drawdown distribution implied by your R-sequence, including paths not yet hit). The concentration test, runnable in ten minutes on a broker statement with no journal required: export closed trades, sum net profit, sort descending and delete the top five trades (or top 5% above 100 trades), then sum the remainder. Worked comparison — Trader A: 240 closed trades, +$41,200 net, top five contributed $28,600, remaining 235 trades still +$12,600. Trader B: 210 closed trades, +$38,000 net, top five contributed $44,000, remaining 205 trades −$6,000. Both headline numbers say "profitable"; only one describes something repeatable at size, and neither trader can tell which they are without the arithmetic. Explicit caveat that some strategies are convex by design — trend following, long-volatility structures, large-move swing approaches — and are supposed to earn most of their return from a small tail, so a Trader B profile is not automatically a defect; the relevant question becomes whether every qualifying signal was taken, because a convex strategy that skips entries cannot catch the tail it depends on, and answering that requires a record of passed-on trades which a broker statement can never contain. The cheapest version that still works: four fields per trade — setup tag, result in R rather than currency, planned risk versus actual risk, and one line of context — taking under a minute per trade, with planned-vs-actual risk singled out as the field traders skip and the one that pays for the habit because it is the only field measuring the trader rather than the market. Sample-size guidance: roughly 30 trades per setup before drawing conclusions and 50+ for confidence, with emphasis that the threshold is per setup, so 300 trades spread across eight setups is thin everywhere. Three cases where the answer is genuinely no, stated without hedging: trading on a desk with its own risk and accounting stack that already computes per-strategy attribution, exposure and drawdown continuously (re-keying into a second tool is duplicate data entry); running fully systematic with a live-versus-backtest comparison pipeline (the infrastructure is the journal); and trading too infrequently for per-setup expectancy to ever say anything (better served by a written thesis record than trade analytics). The common thread is that all three already perform the function under a different name; the position that does not hold up is having none of that infrastructure and substituting confidence for it. Honest import-coverage section rather than an overclaim: MT4 and MT5 live sync via MetaApi including account balance so open positions and equity are current rather than reconstructed at end of day; Tradovate supported for futures, covering many but not all Apex and Topstep accounts; CSV import for everything else including NinjaTrader exports, Rithmic-based setups and most broker statements — with the plain statement that a proprietary in-house desk terminal leaves CSV as the only path and likely places that reader in the "genuinely no" category. Analytics on top of whichever import applies: expectancy and R-distribution per setup, rolling performance against lifetime so decay surfaces early, Monte Carlo (Pro $30/mo) converting the logged R-sequence into a drawdown distribution instead of a single lived worst case, and balance-aware distance-to-drawdown-limit tracking for funded accounts. Closes by conceding that a reader who has run the concentration test, knows their per-setup expectancy, and can say which way their edge is trending has already been journaling and did not need software to do it. Sourced from outreach conversations with several hundred prop, forex and futures traders. FAQ: do I need a trading journal if I am already profitable, is a trading journal actually worth the time, how many trades before journal data means anything, what is the minimum to log per trade, do professional and prop desk traders keep journals.

### Blog: FTMO Trailing vs. Static Drawdown: The Reset Clock Trap
URL: https://sgnldk.com/blog/ftmo-trailing-vs-static-drawdown/
Target queries: FTMO trailing drawdown, FTMO static drawdown, FTMO 1-step vs 2-step, FTMO max drawdown reset, FTMO end of day drawdown, FTMO drawdown explained
Content: FTMO runs two challenge formats with two different drawdown models, and confusing them blows accounts. The 2-Step Challenge uses a STATIC maximum drawdown: the floor is anchored to the initial balance and does not move, so profit increases the buffer permanently. The 1-Step Challenge uses a TRAILING maximum drawdown that follows the account's equity high upward on an end-of-day basis, so gains raise the floor beneath you and giving those gains back shrinks the buffer even though the balance returned to where it started. Worked $100K examples for each model show how the same sequence of trades produces different survival outcomes depending on format. The 'reset clock trap' is the core of the article: traders assume a single mental model of 'drawdown' and carry it between formats, or assume the trailing floor updates intraday when it updates end of day (or the reverse), and size accordingly. Covers why the drawdown model must drive position sizing rather than being an afterthought — a trailing floor effectively shrinks available risk per trade after a run-up, which inverts the usual instinct to press when winning — and what a journal must display for each model: for static, distance from the fixed floor; for trailing, the running end-of-day high-water mark plus distance beneath it, and peak-to-close giveback per session. Numbers and mechanics hedged as subject to change; verify with FTMO directly. FAQ: does FTMO use trailing or static drawdown, does the 1-Step have a trailing drawdown, does it update intraday or end of day, does maximum drawdown reset daily, and how the 1-Step and 2-Step daily loss limits differ.

### Blog: Liquidity Hunts: Why Your Stop Gets Hit Right Before the Reversal
URL: https://sgnldk.com/blog/liquidity-hunt-trading/
Target queries: liquidity hunt, liquidity grab, stop hunt trading, stop loss hunting, smart money forex, ICT liquidity, prop firm stop loss, why does my stop keep getting hit, equal lows, equal highs
Content: Explains the mechanics behind the pattern where a stop is filled and price immediately reverses, without resorting to conspiracy framing. A liquidity hunt is not a broker targeting an individual account; it is the structural consequence of resting orders clustering at obvious levels. Stop orders sit below equal lows, above equal highs, beneath swing points and around round numbers, and those clusters are exactly where a large participant can find the counterparty volume needed to fill size. Price is drawn to liquidity, takes it, and continues in the original direction — which from the retail seat looks like a targeted stop run. Covers where liquidity pools form and how to identify them before entry, why the effect is especially destructive on a prop firm challenge (a stop-out that would be a normal cost on a personal account consumes finite daily-loss and maximum-drawdown budget that cannot be replenished, so the same event carries asymmetric consequences), and three practical adjustments: placing stops beyond the liquidity pool rather than just inside it and sizing down to keep risk constant, waiting for the sweep and entering on the reclaim rather than anticipating, and avoiding the most obvious level when the structure offers a less crowded alternative. Closes on the journaling angle: a trader's own MAE distribution already contains the evidence — if a large share of losing trades show MAE just beyond the stop before reversing to what would have been a winner, the problem is stop placement relative to liquidity, not the entry signal. FAQ: what a liquidity hunt is, how to stop getting stopped out by them, the difference between a liquidity hunt and a stop run, and why prop firm traders are affected disproportionately.
